subject: biology
title: Nerve impulses
key_idea: A neurone at rest is negative inside, about −70 mV. A stimulus that reaches the threshold opens sodium ion channels and triggers an all-or-nothing action potential. A refractory period follows. Myelin makes the impulse jump between nodes.

blocks.text: A neurone at rest has a potential difference across its membrane. The inside is negative compared with the outside.

items: The resting potential is about −70 mV.
The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out of the neurone and 2 K⁺ in.
This leaves a high Na⁺ concentration outside and a high K⁺ concentration inside.
The membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺, because there are more open potassium ion channels.
K⁺ diffuses out down its concentration gradient, but Na⁺ cannot easily diffuse in.
The result is a net loss of positive charge from the inside, which sets up the electrochemical gradient.

items.meaning: The potential difference across a neurone membrane when it is not conducting an impulse.
The combined effect of a concentration gradient and an electrical gradient on an ion.

items: The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in using ATP.
The membrane is far more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺ at rest.
The inside is about −70 mV relative to the outside.

blocks.text: A stimulus that reaches the threshold opens voltage-gated channels and the membrane potential changes rapidly.

items.text: Some sodium ion channels open and Na⁺ diffuses in, so the membrane starts to depolarise.
If the potential reaches about −50 mV, many more voltage-gated sodium ion channels open. This is positive feedback.
Na⁺ floods in and the inside becomes positive, reaching about +40 mV.
Voltage-gated sodium ion channels close and voltage-gated potassium ion channels open.
K⁺ diffuses out, so the inside becomes negative again.
Too much K⁺ leaves, so the potential dips below −70 mV. Potassium channels then close and the resting potential is restored.

diagram.alt: A line graph of membrane potential against time. It rests, rises sharply to a peak, falls below the resting level, then returns to rest.

items: The all-or-nothing principle: if the stimulus does not reach the threshold, no action potential occurs. If it does, the action potential is always the same size.
A bigger stimulus does not give a bigger action potential. It gives more action potentials per second.
Depolarisation is Na⁺ entering. Repolarisation is K⁺ leaving.
Opening of sodium channels is positive feedback, because Na⁺ entry opens more channels.
An action potential is all or nothing.

blocks.text: After an action potential, the section of membrane cannot be stimulated for a short time.

items: Voltage-gated sodium ion channels are closed and cannot open straight away, so no new action potential can start.
The potassium channels are open, and the resting potential is restored during this time.
This ensures impulses are discrete, with a gap between each one.
It ensures impulses travel in one direction only, because the part of the axon behind cannot fire again.
It limits the frequency of impulses, because a new action potential must wait for recovery.
The refractory period stops a new action potential starting straight away.
It keeps impulses separate and moving in one direction.
It sets a maximum frequency of impulses.

sections.heading: Moving the impulse along the axon

blocks.text: An action potential at one point causes the next point to depolarise, so the impulse moves along the axon.

items: In a non-myelinated axon, local currents of Na⁺ spread to the next section and open its sodium channels. The impulse travels along the whole length of the membrane.
In a myelinated axon, myelin stops ions crossing the membrane, so action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier.
Local circuits of ions carry the depolarisation from one node to the next. The impulse appears to jump, which is called **saltatory conduction**.
Less of the membrane has to depolarise, so the impulse travels much faster.

rows: Less resistance to the flow of ions
Faster when warmer, up to a limit
Ions diffuse faster and enzymes in respiration work faster

items: Saltatory conduction is jumping between nodes of Ranvier.
Myelin, a wider axon and a higher temperature all increase speed.
A non-myelinated axon conducts along its whole length, which is slower.

checks.q: Explain how a resting potential is maintained across the membrane of a neurone.
checks.a: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. The membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺, so K⁺ diffuses out. This makes the inside negative compared with the outside, about −70 mV.

checks.q: Explain what happens when the membrane potential reaches the threshold.
checks.a: Voltage-gated sodium ion channels open and Na⁺ diffuses in. The entry of Na⁺ opens more channels (positive feedback). The inside becomes positive, an action potential results, and it is the same size whatever the stimulus (all or nothing).

checks.q: Give two reasons why the refractory period is important.
checks.a: It makes impulses discrete and separate. It means impulses travel in one direction only. It limits the frequency of impulses (any two).

items: Know the structure of a myelinated motor neurone: cell body, dendrites, axon, Schwann cells, myelin sheath and nodes of Ranvier.
The refractory period must be described as producing discrete impulses and limiting the frequency of impulse transmission.
Know the passage of an action potential along both non-myelinated and myelinated axons.

blocks.text: Explain conduction of an action potential in terms of changes in membrane permeability to sodium and potassium ions, and the role of myelination in saltatory conduction.

items: Describe the resting potential, the events of an action potential and the way the resting potential is restored during the refractory period.
Explain the importance of the refractory period in determining the frequency of impulses: a higher frequency needs a shorter recovery time, and the refractory period sets an upper limit.
Know that the opening of sodium channels in the generation of an action potential is an example of positive feedback.
Know the significance of the frequency of impulse transmission: a stronger stimulus produces more impulses per second, not a bigger impulse.
